name: Bro split

lead: The bro split gives each session to one muscle group, for example chest one day, then back, shoulders, arms and legs. It is a classic bodybuilding arrangement for building size and is widely used in gym culture.

Each muscle gets a lot of volume in one session and is trained directly about once per week. Research summarised on Wikipedia says two sessions per week per muscle produced greater muscle growth than one, while with equal volume frequency did not influence strength. No comparative research ranking the bro split against other splits is cited.

paras: Lifters assign a body part to each weekday and do many exercises and sets for that muscle in the session, usually with the weekend off. It is often combined with progressive overload and a surplus when size is the goal. Results build over months.
No harms specific to the bro split are documented. General resistance-training cautions apply, including overtraining with excessive volume and soreness from long single-muscle sessions.

angle.text: A classic bodybuilding routine that hits one muscle group hard each day to build size. High volume per session is the route to growth. Frequency research found two sessions per week per muscle produced greater growth than one.

lead: The bro split is a weekly training split in which different muscle groups are trained on separate days, typically one group per session. Wikipedia names it as one of the common splits, along with full body, upper/lower and push/pull/legs [1].
The name is slang from lifting communities. Encyclopedic coverage is brief and the split section is flagged as needing a better source; no comparative research on splits is cited [1].

The relevant research concerns training frequency and volume in general: for muscle growth, two sessions per week per muscle group produced greater effects than one, whereas with equal volume frequency did not influence strength [1][2].
infobox: One muscle group focus per session

paras: Wikipedia defines a split as how a trainee divides weekly volume across muscle groups and days and lists the bro split among common examples; some programs alternate splits week to week [1].

Wikipedia's summary reports that more weekly sessions generally yield larger strength gains but that frequency had no influence when total volume was equalized, and that two sessions per week outperformed one for muscle growth, with three versus two unresolved [1][2]. How these findings apply to any single split is not stated by the sources.
No studies found comparing the bro split directly with other splits in the material reviewed. Related research on training frequency is summarised above [1][2].
